Tidings simply means news — information about something that has happened or is happening, especially when that information is being passed from one person to another.

That's the heart of it. If someone brings you tidings, they are bringing you a report, an update, a piece of news about something in the world.
But Wait — It's Not Exactly the Same as "News"

While "tidings" and "news" share the same core meaning, they are not perfectly interchangeable in practice, because tidings has a strong old-fashioned, formal, and literary flavor. In everyday modern conversation, nobody says "Did you hear the tidings?" the way they would say "Did you hear the news?"

You will encounter "tidings" mostly in:

  • Religious texts and scripture (especially the Bible)
  • Old literature, poetry, and historical writing
  • Christmas carols and seasonal greetings
  • Formal or dramatic writing where a writer deliberately wants a solemn or grand tone
  • Phrases and expressions that have been passed down through centuries and stuck around

So think of it this way: "news" is what you say every day; "tidings" is what people said centuries ago, and what writers still reach for when they want to sound weighty, ancient, or ceremonial.

You will almost never see or hear the singular form "tiding." In practice, the word lives almost entirely in its plural form: tidings. This is just a quirk of the English language — like "scissors" or "trousers," it simply exists and is used in the plural, even when referring to a single piece of news.

✅ "She brought tidings of the king's death."
❌ "She brought a tiding of the king's death." (unnatural)
The Two Flavors: Good Tidings and Bad Tidings

Tidings, on their own, are neutral — they are just news. But the word is very commonly paired with an adjective that tells you whether the news is good or bad.

Glad tidings (or good tidings) = good news, joyful news
Ill tidings (or evil tidings, sad tidings) = bad news, unwelcome news

The most famous example of "glad tidings" is from Christmas tradition — "tidings of comfort and joy" — meaning news of happiness and peace. When someone says they bring "glad tidings," they are saying they carry a message of joy.

On the other side, a messenger might arrive with ill tidings — meaning they are about to deliver news of a defeat, a death, or some other unfortunate event.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

The word almost always appears in the context of someone bringing, bearing, carrying, or receiving tidings — because the idea built into the word is that information is traveling from one place or person to another.

Common patterns:

  • "bring tidings" — to deliver news
  • "bear tidings" — same as above, slightly more formal
  • "receive tidings" — to get news
  • "tidings of [something]" — news about a specific event or subject

Examples:

  • "The soldier returned from the front, bearing tidings of victory."
  • "We bring you glad tidings of great joy."
  • "The tidings were grim — the harvest had failed."
  • "No tidings had reached the village for weeks."
  • "She anxiously awaited tidings from her family abroad."

Because "tidings" is plural in form, it takes a plural verb.

✅ "The tidings were welcome."
❌ "The tidings was welcome."

A simple mental anchor: a "tiding" is a piece of news traveling toward you. Tidings are the things a messenger, a letter, or a traveler might carry. The word carries with it an image of a world before phones and internet — where news had to physically travel, carried by a person on horseback or by ship, from the place where something happened to the people who needed to know.

Tidings means news or information about events, used almost always in the plural, with an old-fashioned and formal tone, and most naturally paired with words like glad, ill, good, or sad to tell you whether the news is welcome or not.
